about: Rowan's annotations, an invented case. Every participant turn in order, found by its opening words: its experiential statements and each one's key quote, quote and statement in the same order, a gap in a quote marked with an ellipsis, its exploratory note and the words highlighted, or empty for a turn reviewed and left empty. Then the times of the work and his PET board. make_demo.py builds the workbook, the progress file and the themes file from this and the interview CSV beside it.

es: The dog gone but still in the present tense
turns.en: Tense trouble from the first lines: gone, and still in the present tense. Everything, meant both ways, as warmth and as weight.
kq: She went in the summer, so I keep starting to say it is and then it's was.

es: The dog his best company in a lonely time
Taken over by the dog's needs before he saw it
turns.en: Whole days without speaking, then a dog at his knee. The taking over is only visible once it has happened.
kq: She was the best company I've ever had, honestly, and she came at a point where I didn't have much company. … And then there's this dog leaning on my knee under the desk.
But the other way is that she took over. Everything had to be arranged round her. Every single thing. And I didn't see it happening until it had already happened.

turns.at: So I'd be up at quarter past five.
es: Days pushed into the dark round the dog's fear, not really a joke
turns.en: A timetable built round her fear of other dogs. Scream, not bark: he corrects his own word to give its size.
kq: If she saw one, even right across the park, she'd go up on her back legs and scream at it. Not bark. Scream. … Half five in the morning and then again at eleven at night. Dark at both ends. I used to joke I'd gone nocturnal. I wasn't really joking.

turns.at: Some of them were lovely, actually.
es: Some walks in the frost lovely, and theirs alone
Always listening for another dog, even in the lovely moments
turns.en: Joy and watchfulness in one moment. The lovely walks sit inside the listening, never apart from it.
kq: Some of them were lovely, actually. … And I'd stand in the middle with my coffee and think, this is all right, this is ours.
But I was always listening. Even when she was happy I was listening for a car door, or a jingle, someone else's dog. I never stopped listening, the whole time I had her.

turns.at: No. And I didn't notice I was doing it until after.
es: Strange to find his body still on guard for a dog no longer there
turns.en: The watchfulness outlasts her. He finds it out halfway across the road, in his body before his thinking.
kq: That's the strange bit. … I was halfway across before I thought, what are you doing, you haven't got a dog. My body was still doing it for her.
turns.crux: My body was still doing it for her.

es: The dog's closeness lovely, and confining
turns.en: Tenderness and confinement in one image, the head on the foot. Home narrows to the flat and the car.
kq: Which is lovely, and it was lovely, but it also meant I couldn't really go anywhere. She couldn't be left.

turns.at: Erm. At the time I'd have said it was fine.
es: Life narrowed round the dog, not felt as a loss at the time
turns.en: Someone else names it first. The dog as a good reason, and so nobody asks.
kq: I'd stopped saying yes to things so long ago that people had stopped asking. So it's hard to say what it was like, because I didn't feel it as a loss while it was going on. … The dog was the reason, and it's a good reason, nobody argues with it.

es: Unable to keep the dog, or anyone, safe in that flat
turns.en: The letter in his hand, her weight against his legs. Safety splits two ways and he leaves it split.
kq: And I stood in the hall reading it with Skye leaning on my legs and I thought, I can't keep her safe here. Or I can't keep everyone else safe. One of those.

turns.at: Yeah. I've gone back and forth on which.
es: Taking the blame for a life the dog could not live
turns.en: The blame moves over time, from everyone else to her life to himself. She stays blameless throughout.
kq: I've gone back and forth on which. … That I'd put her in a life she couldn't do. … That wasn't her fault. That was mine.

es: Trying everything, and already knowing the dog needed a different life
turns.en: On the record: he wants it known that he tried. The behaviourist's sentence lands before it ends.
kq: I tried everything first. … Nothing was going to help on the stairs. … And I knew what she meant before she'd finished saying it.

es: Awful and a relief, and still a bit ashamed of the relief
Feeling he was lying to the dog, mad as he knows it is
turns.en: A week of saying nothing. A secret kept from a dog who cannot know it, and still felt as a lie.
kq: Awful. And a relief. Both at once, and I was ashamed of the relief, I still am a bit.
And she'd be doing her loops round the tennis courts and I felt like I was lying to her. Which is mad, she's a dog. But that's what it felt like.

es: Comforted by the dog as if she knew
turns.en: The yes comes before the details. He corrects himself, she did not know, and lets the feeling stand.
kq: And Skye came and put her head in my lap. Like she knew. She didn't know, she just saw me on the floor and came over. But it felt like she knew.

turns.at: I drove her up there myself.
es: Watching the dog go without looking back, as he'd want
turns.en: He wants to take her himself. Not looking back is what you would want, he says, twice over.
kq: and she looked back at me once. Then she went off with the man to see the field. She didn't look back again. Which is what you'd want. I know that's what you'd want.

turns.at: I sat in the car in their yard
es: Emptied by her going, in his arms and in the flat
Keeping the dog's bowl without knowing why
turns.en: Light as in empty, the body again. The bowl is kept under the sink, out of sight and never thrown away.
kq: I just felt very light, like my arms didn't have anything to hold. And then I drove home, and the flat was, it was just a flat.
I've still got her bowl, actually. It's in the cupboard under the sink. I don't know why I've kept it.

es: Still waking at her hour with nothing to get up for
Glad of her photos, and needing to put them face down for a bit
turns.en: The old timetable goes on without her. Good news on the screen, and the screen turned over.
kq: Quiet. Very quiet. I still wake up at quarter past five, three months on. Every day. I lie there and there's nothing to get up for, so I just lie there.
And I look at that and think, good. Good, she's happy. And then I put the phone face down on the table for a bit.

es: Needing to say every day she is better off: not settled
turns.en: He takes his own repetition as a sign. Unsettled, and he knows it.
kq: It's like I'm glad and something else at the same time, and the something else hasn't got a name yet. … But I notice I have to keep saying it. If it was settled I wouldn't need to say it every day, would I.

es: Not knowing if he failed her, and no one to tell him
turns.en: Open, and named as open. A question he does not expect anyone to answer for him.
kq: I think I'd want to know first whether I failed her or whether I did the right thing for her, and I don't know that, and I'm not sure anyone can tell me.

turns.at: Only that she was a good dog.
es: The dog never a problem, only frightened
Still reminded of her by every odd sock
turns.en: He defends her against his own telling. He ends on the sock, small and daily.
kq: She wasn't a problem. She was frightened. There's a difference. With me, in the flat, with the door shut, she was the gentlest thing.
Every morning for eighteen months I got one sock. I still find odd socks in the washing and think of her. Stupid, really.
turns.crux: She wasn't a problem. She was frightened.

turns.at: No. No, I think that's everything.
